blocks.text: The chapter contrasts Baal and crafted images with the God who says he has been Israel’s God since Egypt and sustained the people in the wilderness. Hosea contests the tendency to credit grain, wine, oil, fertility, and security to Baal or rival practices. But the passage should not be used to reconstruct one simple, uniform fertility cult: its concern is the misplaced attribution of life and security, not a detailed description of every religious practice.

Verse 14 is difficult to read with certainty. Its language of ransom from Sheol—the realm of the dead—and redemption from death can sound like a promise of rescue, yet in this chapter’s threat-filled movement it may instead be a taunt or threat against death’s victims. The passage has a complex textual history, and later use of its words in a resurrection argument does not by itself settle what Hosea 13 means in its immediate setting.
